analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the estate tax never got past the Senate Finance Committee, which held one hearing and never voted on it before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have eliminated all federal taxes on transfers of wealth at death and as gifts, including the tax on very large estates. Because only estates above a high threshold owed the tax, nearly all of the benefit would have gone to heirs of the wealthiest families and owners of large businesses. The government would have lost the revenue those taxes raise, requiring higher taxes elsewhere or more borrowing. The bill was introduced, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, received one hearing, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates — the top few percent of households whose estates actually owed the tax — would pay nothing on inheritances that can run into the millions. Owners of large family businesses and farms would avoid forced asset sales to cover the tax. Estate-planning lawyers, accountants, and trust companies would lose a major line of business rather than gain.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the federal estate tax, gift tax, and tax on generation-skipping transfers entirely [S2] [S3].

The bill's own findings acknowledge the tax falls only on large transfers, citing rates of 37 to 55 percent on estates that owed it, and note that such taxes raised only about 1 percent of total federal revenue in fiscal 1994 — meaning the benefit is concentrated while the revenue cost is broadly shared [S3].
Supporters argued repeal would spare family-owned small businesses from having to liquidate assets to pay the tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The repealed taxes raised about 1 percent of federal revenue, so that money would have to be replaced through other taxes, higher deficits, or spending cuts — spreading the cost across everyone while the savings concentrate at the top of the wealth distribution.
analysis.who_pays_short: All federal taxpayers and future budgets

drawbacks.text: Repeal eliminates about 1 percent of federal revenue with no replacement, forcing some combination of higher other taxes, more borrowing, or lower spending [S3].

The estate tax is the most progressive part of the federal tax code: because it applies only above a large threshold, repeal transfers wealth retention almost exclusively to the wealthiest families while spreading the fiscal cost across all taxpayers [S3].

Even supporters concede a large industry of tax accountants and lawyers exists to work around the tax; critics would note this planning industry exists because the tax is avoidable for those with means, undercutting the argument that repeal is needed to spare ordinary families.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go overwhelmingly to heirs of multi-million-dollar estates; the costs — lost revenue funding public services — fall on everyone. Whatever relief repeal offers to some family businesses, the dominant effect is a large, permanent tax cut for the wealthiest households paid for broadly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Senate Finance Committee, got a single hearing in June 1995, and sat there until the 104th Congress ended without ever coming to a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Kyl, joined by Sen. Jesse Helms, introduced the bill on March 27, 1995 [S3] [S5].
Nine Republican senators cosponsored it; no Democrats did [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, whose jurisdiction covers tax bills [S5].
The Finance Committee held hearings on June 7, 1995, printing S.Hrg. 104-89, but took no further action on the bill [S5].
No markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers are better off: the ~1 percent of federal revenue these taxes raise never disappeared, and no offsetting tax increase or deficit was created. Heirs of large estates simply continued to owe the existing tax.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyday taxpayers; large-estate heirs gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: All ten Senate supporters — the sponsor, co-introducer, and nine cosponsors — were Republicans; no Democrat joined, and the bill never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Heirs of the largest estates and the wealthiest households
industries.note: Repeal would exempt multi-million-dollar inheritances from tax, a benefit flowing almost entirely to the top few percent of families. The lost revenue would be borne by taxpayers at large.
Supporters cited businesses forced to sell assets to pay estate taxes; repeal would end that. Most small estates already paid little or no tax, so the main beneficiaries remain large ones.

industries.industry: Estate-planning lawyers, accountants, and trust companies
industries.note: Their services exist largely to manage and minimize these transfer taxes; full repeal removes the problem they are paid to solve. Ordinary people do not buy estate-planning services at this scale, so the loss is not a public gain or loss.
A market of policies sold to cover expected estate tax bills would shrink under repeal. Like estate planning, this is a niche product for wealthy families rather than the general public.
